full_judgment:
2. The opposite party No. 1 to 4 filed pre-emption case being No. 4 of 2000 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Pirojpur impleading the petitioner and others as opposite party for pre-emption. The case of the plaintiffs in short is that SA Khatian No. 1259/1360/1261/1262/1263/1271/1315/1316/ 1356/1357/1343/1443/1444/1450/1455/444 of Mouza Nadmulla PS Bhandarin District Pirojpur originally belongs to Alfatunessa and she transferred the same on 7-9-1973 in favour of opposite party No. 4 Habibunnessa and opposite party No. 5. Shamaul Haque by registered Heba-bil-Ewaz deed and delivered the possession, that opposite party No. 5 on 21-3-1978, 4-4-1983, 10-11-88 transferred in favour of pre-emptor Nos. 1-4 by registered Heba-bil-Ewaj deed and in that way the pre-emptors are co-sharer of the suit land; that opposite Nos. 3 and 4 on 30-6-99 transferred 3.20 acres of land to the petitioners by registered deed of 'K' schedule land in the application for an amount of Taka 3,9000 that the opposite party Nos. 1-4 weir not aware of the sale, that the pre-emptee petitioners are stranger in the suit land; that the notices as stipulated in law were not served upon the pre-emptor and on 28-1-2000 thus came to learnt through opposite party No. 3/4 that they have transferred their land. On searching they obtained certified copy of the deeds on 8-2-2002 and confirmed the sale, that SA Khatian No. 609, 610 and 1456 with other khatian containing 3.20 acres transferred in the kabala deed; which compelled preemptors Nos. 1-4 to file the pre-emption case and subsequently after reply of interrogatories the application has been amended on 10-7-2001 and claimed for pre-emption of 2.36 acres land. 

 6. Mr Harunur Rashid, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court without applying their judicial mind and without considering the facts and circumstances and also by misappreciation of evidence and law most illegally and in an arbitrary manner allowed the pre-emption and thereby the lower appellate Court and the trial Court committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate submits that the Court below committed an error of law by misreading the evidence so far it relates to limitation and also failed to notice that partial pre-emption cannot be allowed as well as the Courts below committed a gross error of law by no complying the provision laid down section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act so far it relates to defect of parties. He submits that admittedly the opposite party are cosharer in khatian Nos. 610 and 609. In support of his contention he referred a decision reported in 16 BLD (AD) 12. 

 12. However, since the petitioner raised the question of partial preemption resulting defect of party before this Court relying upon a decision passed in 16 BLD (AD) 12, I am of the view that this point is to be decided for proper adjudication of the case. The claim of the petitioner is that. despite co-sharer of khatian No. 610 and 609 the pre-emptor did not claim any property under the said khatian and also did not make the co-sharer of that particular khatian as party and thereby the case is hit by principle of partial pre-emption as well as defect of party as laid down in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. On perusal of the decision as referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner reported in 16 BLD (AD) 12 it appears that the same relates to pre-emption of "Sufa" as per the Mohammadan law. The principle's and procedures laid down under the Mohammadan law regarding pre-emption is totally different procedures and the same is not relevant for pre-emption either under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act nor under section 24 of the Non Agricultural of Tenancy Act. The decision as reported in 14 DLR 796 as referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner it appears that the same was considered by our Apex Court in the decision referred by the learned Advocate for the opposite party reported in 43 DLR (AD) 108 wherein their Lordships held. 

 13. In the case of Salimuddin (14 DLR 796). Which was decided by a single Bench, several holdings were sold by one sale deed as a single transaction: a co-sharer in the holdings transferred sought to pre-empt some of the holding out others. It was disallowed by the learned Single Bench on two grounds: one was that the consideration money which was paid in a lump for all the holdings together cannot be split up for the purpose of deposit at the time of filing of the application: and the other was that the "single transaction" covering all the holdings cannot be split up by pick and choose to suit the pre-emptor's purpose causing inconvenience to the purchaser. It appears that the learned Single Judge referred to section 14(2) of the Bengal General Clauses Act, 1899 and observed that the word holding appearing in the statue, namely section 26 (F) BT Act, though singular, includes its plural also i.e. a holding may be road as "holding" as well. Emphasis is found to have been given on the fact that all the holdings sold together under a kabala constituted a single transaction but the section did not speak of any transaction or of any single portion or at instrument; the section speaks of a portion or a share of a holding", In Diam Hossain's case (13 DLR 283), decided under the same state, 26(F) BT Act, another Single Bench took a different view and held that though a holding cannot be split up for the purpose of pre-emptor, such as, by allowing pre-emption of one plot out of several plots comprising the same holding, but when two or more holdings are involved, a co-sharer is a liberty to seek pre-emption of one of the holding leaving out others. In that case two holdings were sold under a kabala, one for a consideration of Taka 600 and the other for a consideration of Taka 400 and pre-emption for one of the two holdings was sought for upon deposit of the consideration for that holding only. That per-emption was allowed in view of the provisional in section 26(F) BT Act that a portion or a share of a holding if transferred, could be pre-empted." 

 14. Also by interpreting section 2(13) read with section 96(1) of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act their Lordships of our Appellate Division observed that right of pre-emption is to be instituted on khatian/holding basis. Also is the case reported in 43 DLR 276 the High Court Division held: 

 "The effect of the above decision is that the right of pre-emption accrues not only holdings-wise but also transaction wise. If several holding are sold by one deed of sale, the pre-emptor must pre-empt the entire transaction if he is a co-sharer in all the holdings. This is not the effect and purpose of section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, as held by several cases cited before. The clear intention of the legislature was to confer a right of pre-emption holding-wise and not transaction wise. Section 13 of the General Clauses Act is inapplicable here, because in the context of section 2(13) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, defining the word "holding", read with section 96(1) of the said Act, the right of pre-emption has not been conferred with reference to the number of properties transferred by of particular deed of 'distinct right has been conferred a in respect of a distinct holding. Section 13 of the General Clauses Act is inapplicable because the subject or context is repugnant."
